title: Pronominal suffixes

objectives.can: Identify a pronominal suffix on a noun or preposition.

explanation.summary: A pronoun can be written as a short ending on a noun or a preposition. On a noun it means 'my', 'your', 'his' and so on; on a preposition it is the object: 'to him', 'from me'. The ending is easy to learn, but it changes the vowels of the word it follows.

sections.heading: An ending that is a pronoun
body: Where English has a separate word, Aramaic often adds an ending. שְׁמֵהּ is 'his name' (Daniel 2:20), from the noun שֻׁם 'name' and the ending -ֵהּ, 'his'. אֱלָהָךְ is 'your God' (Daniel 6:21), from אֱלָהּ and -ָךְ, 'your'. The corpus records such an ending as the feature Suffix, with a person, a gender and a number: 3ms means third person masculine singular ('his'), 2ms second person masculine singular ('your'), 1cs first person common singular ('my') and so on.

The ending changes the vowels of the word it joins: שֻׁם becomes שְׁמֵהּ, and מִן becomes מִנֵּהּ. So when you meet a long word, first look at its last letters for an ending from the table below, take it off, and then look for the noun or preposition that is left.
In the corpus's analysis a noun with a suffix is labelled as a construct, as in the earlier lessons.

sections.heading: The endings on a singular noun
body: The first person singular is -ִי, as in חִסְנִי, 'my power' (Daniel 4:27). The second person masculine singular is -ָךְ, as in אֱלָהָךְ. The third person masculine singular is -ֵהּ, as in שְׁמֵהּ, and the third person feminine singular is -ַהּ, as in שִׁנַּהּ, 'its tooth' (Daniel 7:5).

The plural endings are longer: -ַנָא for 'our' (אֱלָהַנָא, 'our God', Daniel 3:17), -כוֹן for 'your' (אֱלָהֲכוֹן, Daniel 2:47) and -הוֹן for 'their' (אֱלָהֲהוֹן, Daniel 3:28). Ezra spells the last two -כֹם and -הֹם, as in אֱלָהֲכֹם (Ezra 7:17) and אֱלָהֲהֹם (Ezra 5:5). The feminine plural 'their' occurs only on a preposition: 'from them' is מִנְּהֵין (Daniel 2:33).

sections.heading: Suffixes on plural nouns
body: A plural noun takes a slightly different set of endings, with a letter י in them. The best known is -וֹהִי for 'his': עַבְדוֹהִי is 'his servants' (Daniel 3:26), where a singular noun such as שְׁמֵהּ would take -ֵהּ. 'Her' becomes -ַיהּ, as in גַפַּיהּ, 'its wings' (Daniel 7:4), and 'their' -ֵיהוֹן, as in בְּנֵיהוֹן, 'their sons' (Daniel 6:25).

So on a noun -ַי, -ָיךְ, -וֹהִי, -ַיהּ, -ֵיכוֹן and -ֵיהוֹן usually point to a plural noun, and the singular endings above to a singular one. This helps with the number of the noun. The suffix for a feminine 'your' that grammars list does not occur in these texts: there is no feminine 'you' suffix in the corpus at all.

sections.heading: Suffixes on prepositions
body: A preposition with a suffix has the person as its object. לֵהּ is 'to him' (Daniel 2:16); לְהוֹן is 'to them'; מִנֵּהּ is 'from him'; עֲלוֹהִי is 'upon him'; and קָדָמוֹהִי is 'before him' (Daniel 4:5). Prepositions such as עַל, קֳדָם and מִן add the same endings as plural nouns (עֲלוֹהִי, קָדָמוֹהִי) or as singular ones (עֲלָךְ, מִנָּךְ). Learn the common ones by sight.
The particle אִיתַי, 'there is', also takes suffixes: אִיתַנָא is 'we are' (Daniel 3:18), and אִיתֵיכוֹן 'you are' (Daniel 3:14). Pronominal suffixes on verbs are a separate lesson.

misunderstandings: The suffix names the owner, not the thing. In שְׁמֵהּ the ending -ֵהּ means 'his' and the noun is 'name'. In שִׁנַּהּ the ending says that the owner is feminine ('its tooth'), not that the tooth is.
The ending -ֵהּ ('his') and -ַהּ ('her') differ only in the vowel. Look at it carefully.
A long word is not a new word. Take off the ending, and the prefix if there is one (a ל or ב before the noun), and look for the noun.
Not every ending in a grammar occurs here. The feminine 'your' suffixes, and the feminine 'their' on nouns, are not in the texts.

deeper.heading: Why Ezra and Daniel differ
body: Ezra's texts mostly spell these endings -הֹם and -כֹם where Daniel writes -הוֹן and -כוֹן, although -הוֹן also occurs in Ezra. It is a difference of spelling and vowel between the books. It has little effect on reading, and the forms are the same suffix.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: The king answered and said to the Chaldeans: 'The thing is certain with me; if ye make not known unto me the dream and the interpretation thereof, ye shall be cut in pieces, and your houses shall be made a dunghill.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Three suffixes in one verse. מִנִּי is the preposition מִן with the first person singular ending: 'from me'. וּפִשְׁרֵהּ is the noun 'interpretation' with -ֵהּ: 'and its interpretation'. וּבָתֵּיכוֹן is 'and your houses', a plural noun with the ending -ֵיכוֹן ('your', several people).

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Daniel spoke and said: Blessed be the name of God from everlasting even unto everlasting; for wisdom and might are His;

examples.analysis: שְׁמֵהּ is 'his name', and לֵהּ at the end of the verse is the preposition ל with -ֵהּ: 'to him' or 'his'. Both suffixes are third person masculine singular.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the mouth of the burning fiery furnace; he spoke and said: 'Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, ye servants of God Most High, come forth, and come hither.' Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, came forth out of the midst of the fire.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: עַבְדוֹהִי is 'his servants': a plural noun in the construct state with the ending -וֹהִי. The plural noun asks for the longer ending.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: The first was like a lion, and had eagle's wings; I beheld till the wings thereof were plucked off, and it was lifted up from the earth, and made stand upon two feet as a man, and a man's heart was given to it.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The vision of the lion with wings. גַפַּיהּ is 'its wings', a plural noun with -ַיהּ, third person feminine singular, matching the feminine noun for the animal. לַהּ (twice) is ל with -ַהּ, 'to it'.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: לָךְ is the preposition 'to' with the second person masculine singular ending: 'to you'. לֵאלָהָךְ is ל, 'to', plus 'your God' with the same ending. אִיתַנָא is 'there is' with -ַנָא: 'we are'. Three suffixes in one clause.

reading.why: The answer of the three men to the king uses many suffixes in three short verses: 'our God', 'your gods', 'to you', 'we are', and the verb with an object suffix.
